newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori says Lima crisis talks progressing.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori says Lima crisis talks progressing.

text.p: Peru President Alberto Fujimori said on Saturday that some progress had been made in the latest round of "very constructive" talks with Marxist guerrillas holding 72 hostages for more than two months.
But he told reporters negotiations with the Tupac Amaru rebels occupying the Japanese ambassador's residence were still at a preliminary stage and would probably go on for weeks.

"We cannot predict how many more weeks these discussions will take," he said during a tour of a poor Lima district with Japan's talks observer Terusuke Terada. "We are still at a preliminary stage in the conversations. We will make every effort to achieve a fast, peaceful solution."
Fujimori also said he hoped rebel leader Nestor Cerpa would again take part in face-to-face talks with government negotiator Domingo Palermo when discussions continued on Monday morning.
Fujimori said the search for a peaceful end to the 67-day crisis made a "small advance" because Cerpa attended the fourth round of talks on Thursday, which was seen as a breakthrough.
"This was a great advantage because there was no need to use the red phone," he said, referring to a phone link between the residence and the talks site across the street.
It was the first time the rebel leader had left the besieged residence since he and a band of well-armed guerrillas stormed the building on Dec. 17.

Fujimori said the MRTA leader spoke for nearly an hour, putting forth "his point of view, his diverse proposals, even criticising the government." Palermo laid out the government's position, but no agenda was agreed on for formal negotiations.
The rebels are demanding the freeing of 400 jailed comrades. The government has refused to consider the idea but is willing to allow the hostage-takers to seek asylum abroad.

Earlier on Saturday, Fujimori insisted Peru-Japan relations remained on a solid footing despite the crisis. "The cooperation between the government of Peru and the government of Japan at all levels continues normally," he said.

Japan has been broadly supportive of Fujimori. But it has criticised his government for police provocation of the rebels and there is strong speculation that Tokyo's pressure has kept Peru from carrying out a military solution to end the crisis.
MRTA rebels, meanwhile, said in their early morning broadcast on Saturday that they backed a leading human rights group's bid to mediate in the siege talks, local radio said.

A delegation from Mothers of Plaza de Mayo, famous for their struggle against Argentina's military rulers in the 1970s, marched up to the presidential palace on Friday to ask for an interview with the president. No one answered the door.
The Mothers want to visit the hostages as well as jailed MRTA rebels.

On Saturday afternoon, three mediators -- Canada's envoy Anthony Vincent, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Red Cross representative Michel Minnig -- went into the mansion in Lima's swank San Isidro district without speaking to reporters.

Despite progress in establishing talks, Peru on Friday extended for another two months a state of emergency in force around the residence as well as in 12 mainly poor Lima districts thought to be guerrilla hide-outs.
Among the 72 hostages are Fujimori's brother, Pedro, two Peruvian government ministers, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
